data.title: Did Boeing’s Fall Catch You Out? What Investors Missed
data.description:
Boeing just landed a multibillion-dollar contract to build the U.S. Navy's next generation F/A XX fighter, adding another long-dated program to an already large defense backlog. That sounds like the kind of headline long-term holders hope for. Holding Boeing from the start of the year would have meant a 31.6% loss, including dividends. If you had made that call on 1 January 2026, how much of this outcome was really visible in the information on record then?

The Two Boeing Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$217 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Boeing then had two very different stories on the table.

The bullish narrative pointed to a fair value of US$253, a notional price based on assumptions that revenue would grow 14.9% a year and profit margins would reach 6.2% over three years as air travel demand supported a large order backlog.

The bearish view put fair value at US$187, again an implied level, and focused on risks like high debt of about US$53.3b limiting flexibility while certification delays on the 737-7 and 737-10 kept pressure on future profitability.

What The Evidence Did To The Boeing Argument

The F/A XX award and more than US$2b of additional defense work backed the bullish Boeing idea of a deep, long-term backlog. Q3 2026 results also helped that side, with revenue at US$24.2b and the net loss narrowing to US$203m as net margin improved from -23.3% to -0.8%. Profitability still was not proven, so the evidence cut both ways.

The whole episode turned on whether stronger orders would translate into actual earnings. For any other contractor heavy on fixed-price work, you would track backlog growth against net margin in each segment to see whether new deals are arriving faster than execution problems are eating into profit.

What Boeing’s Lower Price Now Asks You To Believe

Boeing shares are now at US$156, leaving holders from the start of the year with a 31.6% loss from the start of the year. The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value above that level, based on what strong programs and cash generation could add up to.

That view leans heavily on a large commercial and defense backlog feeding through to earnings and free cash flow. For the Narrative’s higher figure to be reached, a buyer today would need to assume Boeing can keep production and deliveries humming while gradually improving program profitability.

"Bullish analysts expect Boeing to translate its record commercial and defense backlog, higher production rates, and large next-generation fighter wins into stronger earnings power over time. The main requirement is that Boeing sustain higher 737 and 787 production rates and repair margins in defense and services, while managing supply chain, certification, and labor cost headwinds."

Where Boeing’s Demand Connects Outward

Boeing depends on reliable aircraft systems. Your jets are only useful if the power and hydraulics behind them keep working.

Those same airlines, cargo operators, and militaries also need dependable power gear on the ground. Hangars, maintenance hubs, and airports lean on complex electrical hardware to stay online.

One industrial specialist has pushed hard into that grid side. It builds equipment that controls electricity, manages heat, and helps protect critical infrastructure.

The result is a business wired into the same long-lived projects that benefit Boeing, but from the power and thermal angle instead of the airframe.

data.title: Internity's (WSE:INT) Soft Earnings Are Actually Better Than They Appear
data.description:
Internity S.A.'s (WSE:INT) recent soft profit numbers didn't appear to worry shareholders, as the stock price showed strength. However, we think the company is showing some signs that things are more promising than they seem.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

Examining Cashflow Against Internity's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

Over the twelve months to September 2026, Internity recorded an accrual ratio of -0.28. That implies it has very good cash conversion, and that its earnings in the last year actually significantly understate its free cash flow. In fact, it had free cash flow of zł20m in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of zł8.11m. Internity's free cash flow improved over the last year, which is generally good to see.

Note: we always recommend investors check balance sheet strength. Click here to be taken to our balance sheet analysis of Internity.

Our Take On Internity's Profit Performance

Happily for shareholders, Internity produced plenty of free cash flow to back up its statutory profit numbers. Based on this observation, we consider it possible that Internity's statutory profit actually understates its earnings potential! And the EPS is up 11% annually, over the last three years. At the end of the day, it's essential to consider more than just the factors above, if you want to understand the company properly. In light of this, if you'd like to do more analysis on the company, it's vital to be informed of the risks involved. Examining Cashflow Against Tamex Obiekty Sportowe's Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, Tamex Obiekty Sportowe had an accrual ratio of -2.56. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. In fact, it had free cash flow of zł19m in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of zł4.25m.
